subject: literature
passage: Every morning for eleven years Inés Ramírez had ridden the funicular down the hill to the port, and every morning she had read the newspaper on the way, so that the city below existed for her chiefly as a pause between the shipping notices and the obituaries. It was only on the day the car stalled halfway, swaying a little on its cable while the operator shouted to someone above, that she lowered the paper and looked. The roofs were red and green and rust, stepped down the slope like a crowd on a staircase; washing moved on a hundred lines; and the bay, which she had known as a word on bills of lading, was simply there, wide and absurdly bright. When the car lurched on, she found she had folded the newspaper and could not remember having done so.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A woman realizes that she dislikes her work at the port and wants to leave it.
choices.B: A woman's fear when the funicular suddenly stalls makes her forget about her newspaper.
choices.C: A woman notices that the roofs of her city are painted in a variety of colors.
choices.D: An unexpected delay leads a woman to truly see a city she had long overlooked.

explanation.why: The first sentence establishes that for eleven years the city was only "a pause" in her reading. The stall makes her lower the paper and look, and the description shows her seeing the roofs, the washing, and the bay as real things rather than words on documents. Her folding the paper without noticing confirms how fully her attention has shifted.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about her feelings toward her work.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing suggests fear; her absorption in the view, not alarm, explains why she folds the paper without noticing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The colored roofs are one detail of what she sees, not the point of the passage.
explanation.D: Correct. This joins the setup (years of ignoring the view) to the change the stall produces.
